Adobe’s Cloud Hits First Headwind
Larger deals taking longer to close, but cloud transition still packs a lot of growth ahead
By Dan Gallagher
Sept. 20, 2017 at 12:34 pm ET
The Adobe Systems logo on one of the software maker’s products. LUCY NICHOLSON/REUTERS
Speeding up means speed bumps hurt a bit more. Just ask Adobe Systems
ADBE 0.82% .
Among the older software companies once reliant on plastic compact discs, Adobe
stands out for its relatively rapid transition to the cloud. Five years ago, digital
subscriptions accounted for just 15% of Adobe’s annual revenue. That number now
stands at 84% for the nine-month period ended Sept. 1.
And while that conversion might seem closer to the end than the beginning, Adobe’s
https://www.wsj.com/articles/adobes-cloud-hits-first-headwind-1505925258 Page 1 of 3
Adobe’s Cloud Hits First Headwind - WSJ 2026-08-30, 1:16 AM
business keeps accelerating. The company’s fiscal third quarter results posted
Tuesday marked the ninth consecutive period of revenues growing more than 20% on
a year-over-year basis—a rate the company hasn’t seen in at least a decade.
Profitability continues to improve as well; operating margins came in at 30% for the
quarter compared with 20% just two years ago.
But in corporate tech, bigger sales get more eyeballs. Adobe warned in its earnings
call Wednesday that some larger deals for its Experience Cloud service were taking
longer to close, leading it to lower its near-term outlook for that business. Closing the
deals is more a matter of when than if, according to the company’s explanation. But
with a stock already up 50% for the year and fetching a generous multiple of 35 times
adjusted forward earnings, investors were more primed to take some profits. Adobe’s
share price slipped nearly 4% Wednesday.
Experience Cloud includes most of Adobe’s software used by companies to plan
marketing campaigns. It is smaller than the flagship Creative Cloud business, but has
been a steady growth driver as more companies shift this activity online. Experience
Cloud now accounts for a little over one-quarter of Adobe’s total sales, and Adam Holt
of MoffettNathanson projects revenue for that service will jump 45% over the next two
years. That means plenty more fuel to keep Adobe in the race.

HEARD ON THE STREET Follow
Can Adobe Keep the Clouds Away?
Software maker’s solid performance should help as rising peer valuations will make
investors pickier
By Dan Gallagher
Dec. 15, 2017 at 11:55 am ET
Investors have embraced Adobe’s transition to a cloud-based, subscription business model. LUCY NICHOLSON/
REUTERS
When it comes to software, investors sometimes get what they are willing to pay for.
Adobe Systems has never been a cheap stock to own. It has averaged about 32 times
forward earnings over the past five years, compared with an average of 18 times for
the S&P 500 Software & Services group. The stock trades around that level now, after
having gained about 70% this year as investors embraced the company’s transition to
a cloud-based, subscription business model, which has boosted both revenue and
operating earnings.
https://www.wsj.com/articles/can-adobe-keep-the-clouds-away-1513356909 Page 1 of 3
Can Adobe Keep the Clouds Away? - WSJ 2026-08-30, 1:17 AM
Adobe’s fiscal fourth-quarter results posted Thursday suggests the steam hasn’t yet
run out on that shift. Revenue jumped 25% year over year and exceeded the $2 billion
mark for the first time. Operating margins of 32% were the highest in at least seven
years, according to S&P Global Market Intelligence. Adobe also projected revenue
growth of 21% year over year for the current quarter, which ends in February, and
maintained a previous forecast for full-year growth of 20%.
That should also cool some of the fears that arose over Adobe following its last report,
when the company warned that some larger deals were taking longer to close. With
84% of its revenue now coming from subscriptions, Adobe is showing that strong
growth is still possible at what might seem the tail end of its transition, as demand for
the company’s content and marketing services continues to grow from big and small
businesses.
But Adobe and its peers may still face a higher bar heading into the new year.
Software stocks have been on a tear this year, especially those selling cloud-based and
subscription-based services. The 10 largest cloud software stocks on the market are
up 68% this year—more than double the Nasdaq Composite’s gain. J.P. Morgan’s
software analysts downgraded 19 stocks, including Adobe, earlier this week, citing the
belief that a repeat performance for the sector will be difficult for the coming year.
That will keep the pressure on Adobe to keep up its pace. The company’s solid
performance to date has rightfully made it one of the brightest spots in the cloud
sector. That should give some protection when the rains come.
